title: Adaptive Windowed Iterators and Graceful Roll‑Forward for SDKs (Python/TS/Go)
creator: Maya Thompson
description: High-level PRD for introducing an 'adaptive windowed iterator' primitive across Redwood SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go). The feature combines token/window-based pagination with resumable streaming semantics and an explicit roll-forward mode to improve reliability for long-running fetches and streaming consumers while preserving backward compatibility for existing cursor APIs.
background: Customers build features that require continuous consumption of model outputs or large paginated result sets (logs, evaluations, long chat history). Current SDKs support cursors and resumable streams, but we observe edge cases: cursor expiry during client disconnects, repeated duplicate records on reconnection, poor backpressure handling in high-throughput consumers, and fragmented multi-lang behavior between SDKs.
problem_statement: We need a single, well-specified client primitive that: (1) supports windowed paging by token/time/size, (2) provides a deterministic roll-forward policy that avoids duplicates across reconnects, (3) exposes backpressure hooks for streaming consumers, and (4) is implemented consistently across Python/TS/Go with clear migration guidance and minimal breaking changes.
goals: Define API surface for Adaptive Windowed Iterator (AWI) in Python, TypeScript, and Go
Specify server/client handshake for resumable streams with opaque resume tokens
Add configurable roll-forward semantics (strict-idempotent, best-effort, skip-ahead) with defaults that minimize duplicate downstream processing
Expose backpressure and batching controls to applications (max_window_size, max_bytes, time_window_ms, auto_ack)
Ship SDK implementations and cross-language integration tests covering reconnect, duplicate suppression, and latency/cost regressions
non_goals: Rewriting server-side cursor semantics or storage (server remains backward compatible)
Adding new persistence guarantees for customer data beyond current SLAs
Replacing all existing iterator APIs immediately — migration path instead
proposed_api_changes:
Provide concrete method signatures and options for each language: 
- Python: client.iter_windowed(resource, window_size=100, window_bytes=None, time_window_ms=200, resume_token=None, roll_forward='best_effort', auto_ack=True) -> AsyncIterator[Window] 
- TypeScript: client.iterWindowed(resource, {windowSize, windowBytes, timeWindowMs, resumeToken, rollForward, autoAck}) : AsyncIterable<Window> 
- Go: client.IterWindowed(ctx, resource, IterOptions) -> (<-chan Window, ResumeToken, error) 
Windows contain: items[], start_cursor, end_cursor, resume_token (opaque). Handshake extension: initial request MAY include client_capabilities: {supports_awis:true, desired_roll_forward:'strict-idempotent'}. Server can respond with accepted_policy and server_resume_hint. Clients must tolerate absence of resume_token (legacy servers) and fall back to existing cursor behavior.
acceptance_criteria: AWI APIs implemented in Python/TS/Go with matching semantics and examples in SDK docs
Cross-language integration test matrix passes: reconnect with network drop -> no more than one duplicate window for strict-idempotent; no duplicates for strict-idempotent under normal reconnects
Performance: median per-window latency overhead <= 5% vs baseline iterator; 95th percentile token cost delta <= 3%
Backpressure: client options cap throughput to expected window_size/time_window_ms and prevent unbounded memory growth in standard consumer patterns
Backward compatibility: existing cursor-based APIs continue to work unchanged when clients do not opt into AWI; migration guide published
Documentation: PRD, API reference, quickstart examples, and migration guide are published and linked from SDK homepages
Telemetry: events emitted for connect/disconnect/resume_token_issued/roll_forward_policy_applied and dashboards created in Console showing adoption and error rates
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (internal alpha): implement and run integration tests with internal ingestion services. Phase 2 (beta): release Python+TS AWI behind a feature flag; collect telemetry and developer feedback. Phase 3 (GA): release Go implementation, enable by default for new iterator endpoints, provide opt-in migration for existing endpoints. Post-GA: monitor adoption and tighten default roll-forward to strict-idempotent only if server-side performance validated.
migration_notes: Existing users keep current cursor semantics. Migration steps: (1) update SDK to >= 2026.03 with AWI API, (2) switch to iter_windowed with rollout conservative options (window_size=100, roll_forward='best_effort'), (3) test reconnect scenarios against staging to validate resume_token issuance and duplicate behavior, (4) optionally migrate to strict-idempotent when server supports stable resume tokens. Provide code snippets for Python/TS/Go and a migration checklist.
compatibility_strategy: Design AWI to be opt-in. Handshake indicates support; servers that do not return resume_token are treated as legacy and clients fall back. We will publish a compatibility matrix listing server versions that fully support strict-idempotent roll-forward. SDKs provide compatibility shims (awifiable cursor wrappers) to minimize client code changes.
test_plan: Unit tests for language-specific AWI helpers and edge cases (empty windows, partial final window)
Integration tests simulating network partitions and reconnects across all SDKs
Property tests that verify duplicate suppression properties under different roll_forward policies
Load tests to validate backpressure and memory behavior with high throughput producers
End-to-end compatibility tests against legacy server versions to confirm graceful fallback
open_questions: Should the default roll_forward be 'best_effort' or 'strict-idempotent' for GA?
How should resume tokens be invalidated or rotated for security — short-lived tokens vs. opaque long-lived hints?
Do we need a server-side ledger to guarantee no duplicates for strict-idempotent, or can tokens + idempotent dedupe be sufficient?
What is the recommended retention time for resume_token telemetry to support debugging without violating retention policies?
notes: Implementation trade-offs: strict-idempotent provides strongest guarantees but may increase server state and cost (server must issue stable tokens and retain idempotency hints). Best-effort minimizes server state but can produce duplicates under some failure modes. Default choices aim to balance operational cost and customer expectations; we'll revisit after beta telemetry. Design review scheduled with runtime, infra, and security teams.
